entities.name: Chungmok
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Chungmok (충목왕, 1337–1348), born Wang Hŭn, was the 29th king of the Goryeo Dynasty of Korea, ascending the throne at age seven in 1344 under the regency of his mother, Queen Dowager Myeonghye. His reign of four years coincided with the height of Mongol Yuan influence over Korean politics.

The Yuan dynasty had effectively made Goryeo kings subordinate clients since the 1270s, and Chungmok, like his predecessors, was raised partly at the Mongol court in Dadu (Beijing). His short reign saw the Buddhist monastery system reach its greatest extent in Korea, with royal patronage producing a substantial body of Buddhist manuscripts and temple construction across the peninsula. Chungmok's court maintained the Goryeo tradition of Buddhist state patronage even as Yuan power was beginning to fracture under internal pressures that would lead to the dynasty's collapse in 1368.

He died in 1348 at the age of twelve, likely of illness, leaving no heirs. His premature death was part of a broader pattern of short reigns and dynastic instability that characterized late Goryeo under Mongol suzerainty. The institutional framework he helped maintain — a well-organized Buddhist sangha, literate monks capable of manuscript production, and a court culture combining Goryeo and Mongol aesthetic traditions — helped preserve Korean literary and artistic culture through the subsequent turmoil of the late Goryeo period and the dynastic transition to Joseon in 1392.
